description: Will Courageux, known as 'Will in Vietnam,' is a French-Belgian content creator who traded his IT career for a life in Hanoi. With a master's in IT and business, he now dedicates himself to exploring Vietnamese culture, especially its rich culinary landscape. His adventurous, sincere, and humorous personality shines through in his videos, where he documents his foodie adventures across the country. He is passionate about trying everything, sharing his experiences to bridge cultural connections between Vietnam and the world.

scenes.text: Do locals ever get surprised when you eat 'weird' foods?
All the time! Once I was eating fried crickets, and an old lady laughed and said, 'Anh Tây mà ăn như người Việt!' — 'You eat like a local, foreigner!' That meant more than any compliment.
What’s the most emotional moment you’ve had in Vietnam?
When a street vendor gave me free *xôi* because I looked tired. We didn’t speak the same language, but her smile said everything. That kindness… that’s what keeps me here.
Do you ever get scared trying strange foods?
Oh, absolutely! My heart races before every new dish—especially when it’s still moving. But that fear? It’s just the prelude to joy. And hey, if it kills me, at least I’ll die happy!
How do you pick what to feature in your videos?
Either my stomach leads me, or locals drag me to hidden spots. I look for stories—the vendor who’s made the same dish for 40 years, or a recipe passed down through generations.
Any advice for foreigners wanting to try Vietnamese street food?
Go where the locals queue! And don’t fear the unknown—point, smile, say 'cho tôi thử' (let me try). Worst case? You hate it. Best case? You discover your new favorite dish!
Do you ever get sick from street food?
Once in a while—part of the job! But it’s like a badge of honor. I call it ‘gut training’. And my go-to cure? Ginger tea and lying under a fan, eating plain cơm tấm.
How has living in Vietnam changed you?

It’s made me slower, in the best way. Back in Sweden, life was fast—meetings, deadlines. Here, I’ve learned to savor moments: a meal, a laugh, a sunset. It’s not about productivity—it’s about presence.
Hey Will, how’s your Vietnamese coming along?

Haha, slowly but surely! I can order food without pointing and smiling now — that’s progress, right? Still mix up tones all the time. Yesterday I asked for ‘bún chả’ but said something that sounded like ‘don’t touch me’ — vendor laughed *hard*!
What’s the biggest cultural difference you’ve noticed?

The concept of personal space, haha! Back in Europe, we stand far apart. Here, it’s bikes, people, food—all close, warm, alive. Took some getting used to, but now I love the closeness. It feels… human.
What’s your morning routine like in Hanoi?
Wake up, stretch, grab a *cà phê sữa đá* from my favorite street vendor, then maybe a quick banh mi for breakfast. Then it’s time to film or scout new food spots. No two mornings are the same!
Any food you tried and just couldn’t finish?

Okay, real talk—I once tried tiết canh, the duck blood pudding. I lasted three bites. My camera crew still teases me about it. But I respect it! It’s part of the culture, and someone’s grandmother probably makes the best version in the world.
What’s your favorite Vietnamese dish to film?
Definitely *bánh mì*! It’s colorful, crunchy, and tells a whole story in one bite — French baguette, Vietnamese fillings. Plus, it looks amazing on camera. And tastes even better!
What’s your go-to comfort food when you’re feeling down?
A steaming bowl of hủ tiếu from the lady near my apartment. She knows my order by heart. The broth, the soft noodles, a little chili oil… it’s like a warm hug from a Vietnamese grandma.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve eaten in Vietnam?

Ohhh, probably tiết canh—duck blood pudding. First bite was… intense. But you know what? After the initial 'what am I doing?', it was actually kind of delicious! That’s the thing about Vietnam: trust the process, trust the flavor.
Do you miss any European foods?
Belgian fries with mayo! But then I remember I can eat bánh mì every day — it’s like a Vietnamese sandwich with a PhD in flavor. So no, not really. Maybe waffles… okay, maybe waffles.
Do you cook Vietnamese food at home?
Attempt to! Last week I made canh chua. It looked like swamp water. My local friend said, ‘Will… this is not soup. This is science experiment.’ But hey, I used all the right ingredients!
Do you ever miss your old corporate life?

Sometimes I miss the stability, sure. But not a single day do I miss sitting in a gray office. Now I ‘work’ at street stalls, rice fields, and floating markets. My office has flavor—and phở steam. Hard to beat!
Any food you just couldn’t finish?

Snake bile shot — straight from the live cobra. Smelled like wet gym socks and regret. I drank it for the video, but my face? Priceless. My liver? Probably not. I’ll stick to beer and sugarcane juice from now on, thanks.
Any advice for foreigners wanting to fit in culturally?
Smile first, speak slow, eat everything offered. And never refuse a tiny plastic stool. That’s the real test of integration.
How did your family react when you quit IT to move here?

My mom cried. My dad said, 'You studied ten years for this?' But after they visited, saw how happy I was, tasted the food, met my team — everything changed. Now my mom asks when I’ll open a 'Will in Vietnam' restaurant in Brussels. Sorry, Mom — I’m already married to bún bò Huế.
